name: Ten Finger Guillotine from Guillotine Control
description: Master the Ten Finger Guillotine from Guillotine Control in BJJ. Setup, grip mechanics, finishing details, and defensive counters for this high-percentage choke.
summary: The Ten Finger Guillotine from Guillotine Control is a blood choke finished by interlacing all ten fingers around an opponent's already-controlled neck, exploiting the pre-established head control to set choking depth before locking the strongest possible grip.
overview:
The Ten Finger Guillotine from Guillotine Control is a high-percentage choke that leverages the already-established head and neck control of the guillotine position to apply a devastatingly tight interlocking finger grip. Unlike catching the ten finger guillotine during scrambles or from front headlock, executing it from Guillotine Control means the attacker has already broken the opponent's posture, secured hip-to-hip connection, and eliminated the primary escape vectors. This pre-existing control transforms the ten finger grip from an opportunistic catch into a methodical finishing sequence.

The key distinction from other guillotine entries is the ability to pre-load choking pressure before interlacing the fingers. From Guillotine Control, the attacker can first establish the choking arm depth, adjust the forearm blade across the trachea and carotid arteries, and only then transition to the ten finger grip when alignment is optimal. This sequencing dramatically increases finish rate because the opponent is already defending posture and position before the final grip locks in. The interlaced fingers create a unified compression system that is extremely difficult to peel or strip compared to gable or S-grip alternatives.

Strategically, this submission chains naturally with the broader guillotine control attack system. If the opponent defends the ten finger grip by hand fighting, the attacker can transition to high elbow guillotine, arm-in guillotine, or use the choke threat to advance to mount or side control. The position rewards patience—the attacker who takes time to establish proper depth and alignment before committing to the finish will have a substantially higher success rate than one who rushes the grip change.

injury_risks.injury: Trachea damage from excessive crushing pressure
injury_risks.recovery_time: 2-4 weeks with severe cases requiring medical attention

injury_risks.injury: Neck strain or cervical spine stress from jerking motions
Loss of consciousness from carotid compression
injury_risks.recovery_time: Immediate recovery but repeated incidents can cause long-term damage

injury_risks.injury: Jaw or temporomandibular joint (TMJ) injury from improper chin positioning

safety_considerations.application_speed: SLOW and progressive - 3-5 seconds minimum to allow partner to recognize danger and tap
tap_signals: Verbal tap (saying 'tap' or any distress sound)
Physical hand tap on partner's body or mat
Physical foot tap on mat or partner
Any unusual body stiffening or loss of resistance indicating unconsciousness
release_protocol: Immediately release the choking hand grip while maintaining head control
Lower opponent's head gently to prevent whiplash or neck strain
Create space by stepping back or opening guard to remove all pressure
Check partner's awareness and allow recovery time before continuing
If partner was unconscious, elevate legs and monitor breathing
training_restrictions: Never apply full pressure at competition speed in training - always give partner time to tap
Never jerk or spike the choke with explosive movements
Never continue pressure after partner taps or shows distress
Never practice on partners with neck injuries without medical clearance
Always ensure partner has access to tap with at least one hand free

variations_and_setups.variation_name: Standing Ten Finger from Guillotine Control
variations_and_setups.description: Applied while both practitioners are standing with the attacker having already secured guillotine control. The standing variation uses gravity and hip positioning to amplify choking pressure, with the attacker stepping back and dropping their weight to increase compression on the neck.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When you have guillotine control in the clinch and opponent is too heavy to pull guard with, or when you want to finish before going to the ground

variations_and_setups.description: Executed after pulling guard from guillotine control or when the opponent drives into closed guard. The legs create a fulcrum on the opponent's back, amplifying the squeezing pressure of the interlocked fingers. Hip elevation and back arch generate additional compression without requiring raw grip strength.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When opponent drives you to your back from guillotine control or you pull guard to maximize finishing leverage

variations_and_setups.description: Applied from guillotine control top position while sprawling or maintaining top pressure. The attacker uses body weight and downward hip pressure to prevent guard closure while the ten finger grip closes the choke. Requires careful balance between maintaining top position and generating choking compression.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When you have guillotine control from top and want to finish without conceding guard position

attacker.name: Ten Finger Guillotine from Guillotine Control Attacker
attacker.description: How to finish the Ten Finger Guillotine from Guillotine Control. Grip mechanics, finishing sequence, and counter-responses for this choke.
attacker.overview: Attacking with the Ten Finger Guillotine from Guillotine Control requires a systematic approach that prioritizes grip depth and alignment before committing to the interlocked finger configuration. Because Guillotine Control is already established, the attacker's primary task shifts from catching the neck to optimizing the choking angle and sealing the finish. The interlaced ten finger grip creates a unified compression ring around the neck that is extremely resistant to hand fighting and peeling defenses. The attacker must coordinate upper body squeeze with lower body control—whether through closed guard, sprawl pressure, or hip positioning—to prevent the opponent from creating the space needed to posture out or extract their head. Timing the grip transition from initial guillotine control to the ten finger configuration is the critical skill that separates successful finishes from lost positions.
key_principles: Establish maximum choking arm depth before transitioning to ten finger grip—the forearm blade must cross the centerline of the throat
Keep elbows pinned to your ribcage throughout the finish to eliminate any gap between your arm and the opponent's neck
Use lat engagement and shoulder shrug rather than bicep strength to generate primary choking compression
Maintain heavy hip pressure or closed guard connection to prevent opponent from creating posture or extraction space
Adjust the angle of compression based on opponent's chin position—attack below the chin, never across it
Transition smoothly between ten finger grip and alternative guillotine variations when opponent's defense creates openings
setup_requirements: Guillotine Control already established with choking arm wrapped around opponent's neck and posture broken
Opponent's head positioned below their hips with limited ability to posture up or create space
Choking arm deep enough that the blade of the forearm crosses the front of the throat, not resting on chin or shoulder
Non-choking hand free and available to transition to ten finger interlocking configuration
Lower body control established through guard, sprawl, or hip pressure to prevent opponent backing out

execution_steps.description: Before transitioning to the ten finger grip, confirm your choking arm is positioned deep around the opponent's neck with the blade of your forearm crossing the trachea and carotid arteries. Your armpit should be tight over the crown of their head. If the arm is shallow, use hip movement and shoulder pressure to walk it deeper before proceeding.

Pull the opponent's head down toward your chest using the existing guillotine control grip while simultaneously closing any remaining space with your hips. From top position, sprawl your hips forward and drive your chest weight onto their upper back. From guard, elevate your hips and pull their head into your sternum. Their forehead should be pressed against your chest.

execution_steps.action: Thread non-choking hand to meet choking hand
execution_steps.description: Reach your non-choking hand underneath the opponent's torso to meet your choking hand. Route the hand along the path of least resistance—typically underneath their far armpit or along their chest. Maintain constant downward pressure with your choking arm throughout this transition to prevent any posture recovery during the grip change.

Weave all ten fingers together in a palm-to-palm prayer-style configuration with maximum finger engagement. The fingers should be tightly interlaced with no gaps between them. Position the locked grip so your choking forearm remains centered on the throat structures, not displaced to either side. This grip is significantly stronger than gable or S-grip alternatives and resists peeling attempts.

Initiate the choking squeeze by shrugging your shoulders upward toward your ears while simultaneously pulling your elbows down and back toward your own hips. This creates a powerful constriction that closes the ring around the opponent's neck. The primary force should come from your latissimus dorsi muscles, not your biceps. Think of trying to touch your elbows together behind your back while the hands stay stationary.

Add final compression by arching your upper back and expanding your chest outward. This increases the distance between your shoulders and your interlocked hands, further tightening the noose. From guard, simultaneously elevate your hips and pull with your legs to create a two-directional compression. Maintain the squeeze progressively—do not jerk or spike—giving your partner time to tap.

execution_steps.action: Follow opponent's movement and maintain pressure
execution_steps.description: As the opponent begins to react to the choke—attempting to posture, turn, or hand fight—follow their movement with your hips and adjust your angle to maintain optimal compression. If they turn to one side, angle your body to keep the forearm centered. If they attempt to stand, close guard or hook a leg to prevent them from creating upward distance. Persistent, patient pressure is more effective than explosive squeezing.

common_counters.counter: Opponent postures up forcefully and hand fights to peel interlocked fingers
common_counters.your_response: Immediately close guard or drive hips forward to collapse their posture before the grip breaks. If fingers begin separating, transition to gable grip guillotine rather than fighting to maintain the interlace.

common_counters.counter: Opponent tucks chin tightly and turns head to relieve direct throat pressure
common_counters.your_response: Redirect choking pressure behind the jaw line by driving your wrist deeper and angling the squeeze toward the back of the neck. The ten finger grip allows you to adjust angle without losing compression. Alternatively transition to high elbow guillotine which attacks behind the chin.

common_counters.counter: Opponent drives forward aggressively to stack and pass guard while ignoring choke
common_counters.your_response: Use their forward momentum for a hip bump sweep to mount while maintaining the choke grip. Alternatively, sprawl your hips back and redirect their drive to one side using your legs, keeping them off-balance and unable to establish passing pressure.

common_counters.counter: Opponent traps their arm inside the guillotine to create a frame and reduce pressure
common_counters.your_response: The trapped arm actually increases your compression surface. Maintain the ten finger grip and squeeze across both the arm and neck—the arm-in configuration still attacks the carotid effectively. Alternatively, use the arm as a lever by driving their elbow across their own face to increase neck pressure.

common_errors.error: Transitioning to ten finger grip before establishing sufficient choking arm depth
common_errors.consequence: The interlocked fingers lock in a shallow position across the chin or face rather than the throat, producing discomfort but no actual choke, and the rigid grip makes readjustment difficult
common_errors.correction: Always verify forearm blade position across the centerline of the throat before interlacing fingers. Use hip movement and shoulder pressure to walk the arm deeper first. Once fingers are locked, depth cannot be easily adjusted.

common_errors.error: Releasing hip pressure or guard control during the grip transition phase
common_errors.consequence: Opponent uses the momentary lapse to posture up, extract their head, or advance position to side control while the attacker is focused on hand configuration
common_errors.correction: Maintain constant downward head control with the choking arm throughout the entire grip change. Use legs actively to prevent any posture recovery. The grip transition should take one second maximum.

common_errors.error: Squeezing with biceps and forearms instead of engaging lats and shoulder structure
common_errors.consequence: Arms fatigue rapidly within 10-15 seconds, grip weakens progressively, and the choke becomes a war of endurance that the attacker typically loses
common_errors.correction: Initiate squeeze with a shoulder shrug and lat pull motion. Keep elbows pinned to ribs and let skeletal structure transfer force. The lats are much larger and more fatigue-resistant than the biceps.

common_errors.error: Jerking or spiking the choke with explosive force to get a quick finish
common_errors.consequence: High risk of trachea damage and cervical spine injury to training partner. Also mechanically less effective than progressive squeeze because explosive motion creates gaps in compression.
common_errors.correction: Apply pressure progressively over 3-5 seconds. Steady, increasing compression is both safer and mechanically superior to explosive application. The choke should tighten like a vice, not a strike.

common_errors.error: Maintaining static body position while squeezing instead of making micro-adjustments
common_errors.consequence: Opponent settles into a defensive position where they can breathe and manage the pressure indefinitely, leading to a stalling situation where the attacker burns energy without finishing
common_errors.correction: Continuously adjust hip angle, shoulder pressure, and squeeze direction in small increments. Each micro-adjustment disrupts the opponent's defensive equilibrium and creates new choking angles they must address.

common_errors.error: Refusing to transition when opponent successfully defends the ten finger grip
common_errors.consequence: Extended commitment to a defended submission burns energy, allows opponent to improve position, and wastes the offensive initiative that Guillotine Control provides
common_errors.correction: Recognize defensive success within 10-15 seconds and smoothly transition to high elbow guillotine, arm-in variation, positional advancement to mount, or anaconda/darce if opponent turns. Use the threat to create movement, not stalling.

training_progressions.focus: Ten finger interlocking grip configuration and choking pressure generation
training_progressions.description: Practice interlacing all ten fingers from various guillotine control positions without resistance. Focus on speed of grip transition, proper forearm alignment across the throat, and lat-driven squeeze mechanics. Partner provides no resistance—emphasis is purely on hand positioning and muscle engagement patterns. Drill 20 repetitions from each position (standing, guard, top).

training_progressions.focus: Combining grip mechanics with hip positioning and body movement for the complete finish
training_progressions.description: From established Guillotine Control, execute the full finishing sequence against a partner who maintains position but does not actively defend. Focus on coordinating the shoulder shrug, lat engagement, back arch, and hip elevation into one fluid motion. Partner provides feedback on choking pressure quality. Work 5-minute rounds alternating roles.

training_progressions.focus: Maintaining finish through common defensive reactions
training_progressions.description: Partner defends with specific counters one at a time: posture attempts, chin tuck, hand fighting, driving forward. Practice the prescribed response for each counter while maintaining choking pressure. Gradually combine multiple defenses. Partner at 50-70% resistance. Work 3-minute rounds with specific counter assignments per round.

training_progressions.focus: Applying the submission under realistic resistance with transition awareness
training_progressions.description: Start each round with Guillotine Control established. Attacker must finish or transition within 30 seconds. Defender uses full resistance. Attacker practices recognizing when to commit to the ten finger finish versus when to transition to alternative submissions or positional advancement. Track finish rate over multiple rounds to measure improvement.

flashcards.question: What anatomical structures does the Ten Finger Guillotine primarily attack?
flashcards.answer: The Ten Finger Guillotine primarily attacks the carotid arteries on both sides of the neck, restricting blood flow to the brain. The forearm blade also applies compression to the trachea. Proper technique emphasizes bilateral carotid compression (blood choke) over tracheal crushing (air choke) because blood chokes are faster acting, more reliable, and cause less injury to training partners.

flashcards.question: Why must you establish choking arm depth before transitioning to the ten finger interlocking grip?
flashcards.answer: Once all ten fingers are interlaced, the rigid grip structure makes it extremely difficult to adjust arm depth or forearm angle. If you lock the grip while the forearm is positioned too shallow—across the chin or face rather than the throat—you create discomfort but no actual choke. Establishing depth first ensures the forearm blade crosses the centerline of the throat structures before the grip locks the position permanently.

trap: Lock grip first, then sink deep

flashcards.question: Your opponent starts to posture up during your grip transition—what adjustment prevents escape?
flashcards.answer: Immediately close your guard or drive your hips forward to collapse their posture before completing the grip change. The grip transition should never take more than one second, and you must maintain constant downward pressure with your choking arm throughout. If the opponent begins posturing before you can interlace, abandon the ten finger transition and maintain your existing guillotine control grip until you can re-break their posture.

flashcards.question: What is the proper speed of application when finishing the Ten Finger Guillotine in training?
flashcards.answer: The choke must be applied SLOWLY and progressively over a minimum of 3-5 seconds. Never jerk or spike the choke with explosive movements. Progressive squeeze is both safer for your training partner's trachea and cervical spine, and mechanically more effective because steady compression eliminates gaps. The choke should tighten like a vice closing—continuous increasing pressure that gives the opponent time to recognize the danger and tap before injury occurs.

flashcards.question: How should you immediately respond when your partner taps to the Ten Finger Guillotine?
flashcards.answer: Immediately release the interlocked finger grip while maintaining gentle head control to prevent whiplash. Lower the opponent's head gently, create space by stepping back or opening guard to remove all pressure, and check your partner's awareness. If the partner lost consciousness at any point, elevate their legs and monitor breathing. Never hold the choke even briefly after a tap—release must be instantaneous.

trap: Keep squeezing until they go limp

flashcards.question: What muscle groups should generate the primary choking force, and why?
flashcards.answer: The latissimus dorsi muscles and shoulder structure should generate primary choking force through a shrug-and-pull motion, not the biceps and forearms. The lats are much larger muscles with greater endurance capacity, allowing sustained compression over 30+ seconds without fatigue. Bicep-driven squeezing fatigues within 10-15 seconds, causing grip failure. The correct motion is shrugging shoulders toward ears while pulling elbows down and back toward your hips.

flashcards.question: Your opponent successfully tucks their chin to defend the choke—what are your options?
flashcards.answer: Drive the wrist deeper behind the jaw line and angle the squeeze toward the back of the neck to attack behind the chin tuck. The ten finger grip allows angle adjustment without releasing. If this fails, transition to the high elbow guillotine variation which specifically attacks behind the chin by driving the elbow toward the ceiling. You can also use their chin defense as a distraction to advance to mount or side control, exploiting their positional neglect.

plausible: Pull head up to expose neck

flashcards.question: When should you abandon the Ten Finger Guillotine attempt and transition to another attack?
flashcards.answer: If the opponent successfully defends for 10-15 seconds with active hand fighting, posture recovery, or head extraction, transition rather than burning energy on a diminishing-return attempt. Viable transitions include high elbow guillotine, arm-in guillotine, anaconda or darce choke if they turn, or positional advancement to mount or side control using the choking threat as a distraction. The guillotine control position provides multiple offensive options—never become fixated on a single finish.

defender.name: Ten Finger Guillotine from Guillotine Control Defender
defender.description: How to defend and escape the Ten Finger Guillotine from Guillotine Control. Recognition cues, escape timing, and survival techniques.
defender.overview: Defending the Ten Finger Guillotine from Guillotine Control requires early recognition and immediate action because the interlocked ten finger grip is exceptionally difficult to peel or strip once fully established. The defender's window for effective escape narrows rapidly as the attacker transitions from standard guillotine control to the ten finger configuration—this grip change is the critical moment where defensive intervention has the highest success rate. Once the fingers interlace and the squeeze engages, the defender's options shift from proactive escape to survival and damage mitigation. Understanding the sequential nature of this submission—depth establishment, grip transition, squeeze initiation—allows the defender to identify the optimal intervention point and execute the correct defensive response before the choke becomes inescapable.
key_principles: Defend the grip transition before the fingers interlace—this is the highest-percentage window for escape
Maintain posture at all costs by driving the chin up and creating upward shoulder pressure through the attacker's grip
Use two-handed grip fighting to prevent the non-choking hand from reaching the choking hand during transition
Turn your chin toward the choking arm to reduce direct throat exposure and create space for the jaw
Create distance between your neck and the attacker's chest to reduce compression effectiveness
If caught in the choke, tap early—the ten finger grip tightens rapidly and leaves very little margin for late escapes
recognition_cues: Attacker's non-choking hand begins reaching underneath your torso to meet the choking hand—signals imminent grip transition
Attacker adjusts forearm position by walking the choking arm deeper around your neck, repositioning the blade of the forearm across your throat centerline
Attacker's shoulders shrug upward and you feel lat-driven compression beginning to close the ring around your neck
Attacker breaks your posture by pulling your head firmly against their chest while simultaneously closing space with hips or guard

defensive_options.action: Posture up and hand fight before ten finger grip locks
defensive_options.when_to_use: As soon as you feel the attacker's non-choking hand moving to meet the choking hand—this is the primary escape window
defensive_options.if_successful: You break the guillotine control and return to neutral position or top position with the opponent's grip broken
defensive_options.risk: If you posture late and the grip locks, you've wasted energy and the attacker may use your upward momentum to tighten the choke

defensive_options.action: Drive forward aggressively to stack and pass to side control
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the attacker is on their back in guard and you still have enough posture to generate forward pressure through your legs
defensive_options.if_successful: You pass to side control and the choke angle becomes ineffective, potentially setting up Von Flue counter-choke
defensive_options.risk: Driving forward into a fully locked ten finger guillotine in closed guard amplifies the choke pressure—only commit if you can maintain posture throughout

defensive_options.action: Turn chin toward choking arm and swim inside arm through to create frame
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the grip has already locked but the squeeze has not fully engaged—use the transition between grip lock and full compression
defensive_options.if_successful: Your chin and arm create enough space to relieve carotid compression and you can begin working head extraction
defensive_options.risk: Arm inside the guillotine can become trapped, but the arm-in position is generally less dangerous than clean no-arm guillotine

defensive_options.action: Tap immediately if the choke locks in and you feel blood flow restriction
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the ten finger grip is locked, squeeze is engaged, and you feel lightheadedness or tunnel vision beginning
defensive_options.risk: No risk—this is the correct and safe response when the choke is fully locked

escape_paths: Posture up and strip the non-choking hand before it reaches the choking hand, breaking the guillotine control entirely
Drive forward to pass guard and establish side control, making the choke angle ineffective
Turn chin into the choking arm and swim the near-side arm inside the grip to create a frame and relieve pressure
Circle walk to the choking arm side while posturing to reduce the choke angle and create extraction space

favorable_outcomes.how: Strip the non-choking hand during grip transition phase, then posture up forcefully and hand fight to break the choking arm control entirely. Once posture is recovered, use head positioning and shoulder pressure to extract your head from the remaining arm wrap.

Drive forward aggressively while maintaining posture to pass the opponent's guard. As you establish side control, the guillotine angle becomes ineffective. This creates opportunity for Von Flue counter-choke if they maintain the grip, or forces them to release and play guard.

common_errors.error: Waiting until the ten finger grip is fully locked before beginning defensive action
common_errors.consequence: The interlocked fingers create a grip that is nearly impossible to peel or strip once established, leaving only low-percentage survival options and dramatically increasing the likelihood of being submitted
common_errors.correction: React immediately when you feel the non-choking hand moving to meet the choking hand. The grip transition phase is your primary escape window—use it by posturing up, hand fighting, or driving forward before the fingers interlace.

common_errors.error: Pulling head straight backward against the direction of the choke
common_errors.consequence: Pulling backward actually tightens the noose around your neck because it increases the distance between your throat and the attacker's body, amplifying the compression angle of the forearm blade
common_errors.correction: Move your head toward the choking arm side while simultaneously pushing your chin forward into the crook of the attacker's elbow. This reduces the choke angle and creates a pocket of space. Never pull straight back—always angle toward the choking arm.

common_errors.error: Ignoring posture control and focusing only on hand fighting against the grip
common_errors.consequence: Even if you temporarily disrupt the grip, without recovering posture the attacker simply re-establishes the interlace and you've wasted energy without gaining positional advantage. The broken posture keeps you in the danger zone.
common_errors.correction: Prioritize posture recovery over grip fighting. Use your legs to drive upward, straighten your spine, and create distance between your neck and the attacker's chest. Once posture is recovered, the choke loses its primary compression mechanism regardless of grip configuration.

common_errors.error: Refusing to tap when the choke is fully locked due to ego or competition mindset in training
common_errors.consequence: Loss of consciousness can occur within 4-6 seconds of full carotid compression. Repeated unconsciousness episodes carry cumulative neurological risk. The ten finger grip leaves almost no margin for late escapes once the squeeze engages.
common_errors.correction: Tap early and often in training. The ten finger guillotine from guillotine control is one of the highest-percentage finishes in the guillotine family—recognize when the position is lost and preserve your health for the next round.

flashcards.question: How do you recognize that the attacker is transitioning from standard guillotine control to the ten finger grip?
flashcards.answer: The primary cue is feeling the attacker's non-choking hand begin to reach underneath your torso to meet the choking hand. You may also feel the choking arm being adjusted deeper around your neck as the attacker positions the forearm blade across your throat centerline. Additionally, the attacker will often increase downward pressure on your head to break posture before committing to the grip change.

flashcards.question: What is the safest way to tap to the Ten Finger Guillotine to prevent injury?
flashcards.answer: Tap immediately using the clearest available signal—verbal tap (saying 'tap'), physical hand tap on the attacker's body or the mat, or foot tap on the mat. Use multiple signals simultaneously for clarity. Do not wait to see if you can escape once you feel blood flow restriction or lightheadedness beginning. The ten finger grip tightens rapidly and consciousness can be lost within 4-6 seconds of full carotid compression. Tap early in training—there is no benefit to risking unconsciousness.

plausible: Wait to see if escape works
trap: Try to fight through it first

flashcards.question: Why is posture recovery more important than grip fighting when defending the Ten Finger Guillotine?
flashcards.answer: The ten finger interlocked grip is the strongest hand configuration in grappling and is nearly impossible to peel once fully established. Fighting the grip directly wastes energy with minimal chance of success. However, recovering posture—driving your spine upright and creating distance between your neck and the attacker's chest—removes the primary compression mechanism regardless of grip strength. With posture recovered, the choke loses leverage even if the grip remains intact.

trap: Pull down harder on the arm

flashcards.question: What defensive options are available once the ten finger grip has already locked in?
flashcards.answer: Once locked, options are limited but include: turning your chin toward the choking arm to reduce direct throat exposure, swimming your near-side arm inside the grip to create a frame, driving forward to pass guard and change the choke angle, and circle-walking toward the choking arm side while posturing. If none of these work within 5-8 seconds and you feel the squeeze engaging, tap immediately rather than risking unconsciousness.

plausible: Pull straight back to create space
trap: Lie flat and wait it out

flashcards.question: When defending from bottom position while the attacker applies the choke from top, what is your best escape strategy?
flashcards.answer: From bottom when the attacker has top position with the ten finger guillotine, your best strategy is to create frames against the attacker's hips and shoulders to prevent them from closing distance. Use a hip escape to create angle, then work to recover guard by getting your legs involved. If the attacker is in your closed guard attempting the finish, open guard and hip escape to one side to change the choking angle. Avoid lying flat—angle your body to reduce compression effectiveness.

training_progressions.focus: Identifying the grip transition window and early warning cues
training_progressions.description: Partner establishes guillotine control and slowly transitions to ten finger grip at 25% speed. Defender practices recognizing each phase of the transition: arm depth adjustment, non-choking hand movement, and interlacing initiation. Defender calls out each cue verbally without attempting escape. Build awareness of timing windows before adding defensive responses.

training_progressions.focus: Executing defensive responses at the correct moment during the grip transition
training_progressions.description: Partner transitions to ten finger grip at 50% speed. Defender practices posturing up, hand fighting, and driving forward at the moment they feel the non-choking hand move. Success measured by whether defender escapes before fingers interlace. Work 10 repetitions per defensive option with partner feedback on timing accuracy.

training_progressions.focus: Managing the position when the grip is already locked and squeeze is beginning
training_progressions.description: Start with ten finger grip already established but squeeze not yet engaged. Defender practices chin positioning, arm swimming, and posture recovery against progressive resistance. Partner increases squeeze slowly—defender must either escape or tap. Develops judgment for when escape is still possible versus when tapping is the correct response. Work 3-minute rounds.

training_progressions.focus: Defending the complete submission sequence under realistic conditions
training_progressions.description: Partner begins in Guillotine Control with intent to finish via ten finger guillotine at full speed and resistance. Defender must escape or survive for 30 seconds. Track escape success rate across multiple rounds and identify which defensive option produces the best results. Develop personalized defensive strategy based on body type and grappling style.
